body_html:
Spanish phrases for everyday situations are what most learners actually need. Not verb tables, not word lists, but the right words at the right moment: when you meet your partner’s parents, when a neighbor knocks on your door, when a friend is grieving or when you have to write a formal email. After ten years translating between English and Spanish, I have learned that these moments are where language truly matters, and where a few well-chosen phrases make the biggest difference. This guide gathers every situation in one place, with three key phrases for each and a link to a full guide with conversations, cultural notes and a quiz.

Key takeaways
  • Learn Spanish by situation: phrases stick when you know exactly when to use them.
  • Choosing between tú and usted is the first decision in every situation.
  • Politeness in Spanish lives in small words: por favor, disculpe, ¿podría…?
  • The phrases here follow Mexican and Latin American Spanish, with notes where Spain differs.
  • Regional differences are real, but they rarely block understanding.
{{toc}}

Why learn Spanish phrases for everyday situations?

Most of us don’t learn a language to pass a test. We learn it to connect with people. A phrase learned inside its situation comes with everything you need: who says it, how formal it is and what usually comes next. A phrase learned from a list comes with none of that, which is why it so often disappears the moment you need it.

That is why this guide is organized around real moments rather than grammar topics. Each section below covers one area of life. For each situation you get the three phrases I would teach a friend first, and a link to the full guide.

Three principles for every situation

1. Choose tú or usted first

Before you say anything, decide how formal to be. Use tú with friends, partners, children and most people your age in casual settings. Use usted with older people you don’t know well, in formal situations and, in much of Latin America, with your partner’s parents at first. When in doubt, start with usted; people will invite you to switch with Háblame de tú. The full rules are in {{link:tu-vs-usted|tú vs usted}}.

2. Soften what you say

Spanish politeness is built from small softeners: ¿Podría…? (Could you…?), Disculpe que le moleste (Sorry to bother you), Es que… (It’s just that…). They turn a demand into a request. In Mexico in particular, a bare command can sound abrupt even with a smile.

3. Expect warmth

Spanish-speaking cultures often feel warmer and more personal: a kiss on the cheek, questions about your family, goodbyes that take twenty minutes. Matching that warmth with a smile and a few friendly words matters more than perfect grammar.

Love and dating

Romance is one of the most motivating reasons to learn Spanish, and one of the easiest places to make an awkward mistake. Here are the moments from a first date to a love letter. You can say “I miss you” in several ways, all in {{link:how-to-say-i-miss-you-in-spanish|how to say I miss you in Spanish}}, and the difference between the two ways to say “I love you” is in {{link:te-quiero-vs-te-amo|te quiero vs te amo}}.

A first date

Keep it light, ask questions and show interest. The last phrase is how most people in Mexico say they had a good time.

  • ¿Te gustaría salir conmigo el viernes? (Would you like to go out with me on Friday?)
  • ¿Qué te gusta hacer en tu tiempo libre? (What do you like to do in your free time?)
  • La pasé muy bien contigo. (I had a great time with you.)

Full guide: {{link:first-date-in-spanish|first date in Spanish}}.

Flirting

Spanish flirting tends to be direct but warm. A compliment and an invitation go a long way; cheesy pickup lines are a joke even in Spanish.

  • Me encanta tu sonrisa. (I love your smile.)
  • ¿Te puedo invitar un café? (Can I buy you a coffee?)
  • ¿Me das tu número? (Can I have your number?)

Full guide: {{link:how-to-flirt-in-spanish|how to flirt in Spanish}}.

Texting

Spanish texting has its own shorthand and a lot of laughter written as jajaja.

  • tqm (te quiero mucho, love you lots)
  • xq / pq (porque or por qué, because or why)
  • ntp (no te preocupes, don’t worry)

Full guide: {{link:texting-in-spanish|texting in Spanish}}.

Terms of endearment

Spanish speakers use pet names constantly, with partners, children and even friends.

  • mi amor (my love)
  • cariño (sweetheart)
  • mi vida (my life, darling)

Full guide: {{link:spanish-terms-of-endearment|Spanish terms of endearment}}.

Long-distance love

When you can’t be together, the words do the work. In Spain you’ll hear te echo de menos instead of te extraño.

  • Te extraño mucho. (I miss you so much.)
  • Cuento los días para verte. (I’m counting the days until I see you.)
  • Que sueñes bonito. (Sweet dreams.)

Full guide: {{link:long-distance-relationship-spanish|long-distance relationship in Spanish}}.

Apologizing to your partner

A sincere apology in Spanish names the feeling, takes responsibility and avoids excuses.

  • Perdóname, no fue mi intención. (Forgive me, I didn’t mean to.)
  • Tienes razón, me equivoqué. (You’re right, I was wrong.)
  • Lo siento de corazón. (I’m truly sorry.)

Full guide: {{link:apologizing-to-your-partner-in-spanish|apologizing to your partner in Spanish}}.

Writing a love letter

A love letter is where Spanish can be at its most beautiful, and where a simple, honest sentence beats a translated poem.

  • Desde que te conocí, todo es diferente. (Since I met you, everything is different.)
  • Eres lo mejor que me ha pasado. (You’re the best thing that has ever happened to me.)
  • Con todo mi amor (With all my love)

Full guide: {{link:love-letter-in-spanish|how to write a love letter in Spanish}}.

{{image:2}}

Family and your partner’s family

For many learners, the most important Spanish speakers are family: a partner’s parents, grandparents who speak little English, or children growing up with both languages. These guides are written for those moments. For staying close across borders and celebrating together, see {{link:video-calls-with-family-in-spanish|video calls with family in Spanish}} and {{link:spanish-holiday-phrases|Spanish holiday phrases}}.

Meeting your partner’s family

First impressions matter, and formality is your friend. Use usted with parents and grandparents until they invite you to use tú.

  • Mucho gusto, señora. (Nice to meet you, ma’am.)
  • Encantado de conocerlos. (Delighted to meet you all.)
  • Gracias por recibirme en su casa. (Thank you for welcoming me into your home.)

Full guide: {{link:meeting-your-partners-family-in-spanish|meeting your partner’s family in Spanish}}.

Talking to your in-laws

The relationship builds over many visits. Offering help and asking about their lives are the quickest ways in.

  • ¿Le ayudo con algo? (Can I help you with anything?)
  • ¿Cómo ha estado? (How have you been?)
  • Muchas gracias por todo, suegra. (Thank you so much for everything, mother-in-law.)

Full guide: {{link:talking-to-your-in-laws-in-spanish|talking to your in-laws in Spanish}}.

Family dinner

Meals are long and social, and the conversation that lingers afterward has its own name: la sobremesa.

  • ¡Provecho! (Enjoy your meal!)
  • ¿Me pasas la sal, por favor? (Could you pass the salt, please?)
  • Ya no puedo más, gracias. (I couldn’t eat another bite, thank you.)

Full guide: {{link:family-dinner-spanish-phrases|Spanish phrases for family dinner}}.

Complimenting food

Praising the cook is close to obligatory, and going beyond delicioso makes a big impression.

  • ¡Qué rico está todo! (Everything is so good!)
  • ¿Me da la receta? (Could you give me the recipe?)
  • Se me antoja otro taco. (I’m craving another taco.)

Full guide: {{link:how-to-compliment-food-in-spanish|how to compliment food in Spanish}}.

Weddings

From the toast to the dance floor, a few phrases let you celebrate like family.

  • ¡Felicidades a los novios! (Congratulations to the couple!)
  • Quiero brindar por… (I’d like to raise a toast to…)
  • ¡Que vivan los novios! (Long live the bride and groom!)

Full guide: {{link:spanish-wedding-phrases|Spanish wedding phrases}}.

Talking to kids

Children are the best and most honest teachers. Everyday routines give you the most practice.

  • ¡Ven acá, mi amor! (Come here, sweetheart!)
  • ¿Ya te lavaste los dientes? (Did you brush your teeth?)
  • ¡Qué bien lo hiciste! (You did that so well!)

Full guide: {{link:talking-to-kids-in-spanish|talking to kids in Spanish}}.

{{book:love-slowly}}

Feelings and big moments

The moments that matter most are often emotional, and they are exactly where a translated phrase can sound cold or wrong. These guides help you celebrate, support and apologize in a way that sounds sincere. And for every kind of gratitude, see {{link:ways-to-say-thank-you-in-spanish|ways to say thank you in Spanish}}.

Birthday wishes

In Mexico, birthdays come with a song, Las Mañanitas, and wishes for many more years.

  • ¡Feliz cumpleaños! (Happy birthday!)
  • ¡Que cumplas muchos más! (Here’s to many more!)
  • Que todos tus deseos se hagan realidad. (May all your wishes come true.)

Full guide: {{link:birthday-wishes-in-spanish|birthday wishes in Spanish}}.

Congratulations

Celebrate a new job, a graduation or a baby. In Spain, ¡Enhorabuena! is the classic choice.

  • ¡Felicidades! (Congratulations!)
  • ¡Te lo mereces! (You deserve it!)
  • Estoy muy orgulloso de ti. (I’m very proud of you.)

Full guide: {{link:congratulations-in-spanish|congratulations in Spanish}}.

Get well soon

A short message to someone who is sick shows you care, whether by text or in person.

  • Que te mejores pronto. (Get well soon.)
  • Cuídate mucho. (Take good care of yourself.)
  • Si necesitas algo, avísame. (If you need anything, let me know.)

Full guide: {{link:get-well-soon-in-spanish|get well soon in Spanish}}.

Condolences

In the hardest moments, simple and sincere words are best. Pésame is the formal word for condolences.

  • Lo siento mucho. (I’m so sorry.)
  • Mi más sentido pésame. (My deepest condolences.)
  • Te acompaño en tu dolor. (I’m with you in your grief.)

Full guide: {{link:condolences-in-spanish|condolences in Spanish}}.

Comforting someone

Sometimes it is not about death, just a bad day, a breakup or a worry. Listening matters more than the perfect phrase.

  • Aquí estoy para ti. (I’m here for you.)
  • ¿Quieres hablar de eso? (Do you want to talk about it?)
  • Todo va a estar bien. (Everything’s going to be okay.)

Full guide: {{link:how-to-comfort-someone-in-spanish|how to comfort someone in Spanish}}.

Talking about feelings

Spanish often describes emotions with verbs like ponerse and dar, not just “I am”.

  • Me siento un poco triste hoy. (I feel a bit sad today.)
  • Me da miedo hablar en público. (Speaking in public scares me.)
  • Me pone nervioso esperar. (Waiting makes me nervous.)

Full guide: {{link:talking-about-feelings-in-spanish|talking about feelings in Spanish}}.

Apologizing

Spanish has three everyday apologies. Perdón is for small slips, disculpe is formal and also used to get attention, and lo siento expresses real regret.

  • Perdón, no te vi. (Sorry, I didn’t see you.)
  • Disculpe, ¿me deja pasar? (Excuse me, may I get by?)
  • Lo siento mucho, fue mi culpa. (I’m very sorry, it was my fault.)

Full guide: {{link:how-to-apologize-in-spanish|how to apologize in Spanish}}.

Everyday life

Daily life is where your Spanish gets the most practice. None of these situations is dramatic, but together they make up most of your real conversations. Two more errands are covered in {{link:grocery-shopping-in-spanish|grocery shopping in Spanish}} and {{link:at-the-pharmacy-in-spanish|at the pharmacy in Spanish}}.

Small talk

Elevators, waiting rooms and coffee lines are perfect for short, friendly exchanges.

  • ¿Qué tal tu fin de semana? (How was your weekend?)
  • ¡Qué calor hace hoy! (It’s so hot today!)
  • ¿Y tú, a qué te dedicas? (And what do you do for a living?)

Full guide: {{link:small-talk-in-spanish|small talk in Spanish}}.

Neighbors

A greeting in the hallway builds goodwill that helps when you need a favor, or have to mention a noise problem.

  • Buenos días, vecina. (Good morning, neighbor.)
  • ¿Me podría hacer un favor? (Could you do me a favor?)
  • Disculpe, ¿podría bajarle un poco a la música? (Excuse me, could you turn the music down a little?)

Full guide: {{link:talking-to-neighbors-in-spanish|talking to neighbors in Spanish}}.

Making friends

Turning an acquaintance into a friend usually takes an invitation, and the courage to make it.

  • ¿Quieres tomar un café un día de estos? (Do you want to grab a coffee sometime?)
  • ¿Nos vemos el sábado? (Shall we meet up on Saturday?)
  • Pásame tu WhatsApp. (Send me your WhatsApp.)

Full guide: {{link:making-friends-in-spanish|making friends in Spanish}}.

Phone calls

Phone calls are hard because there are no gestures to help. In Mexico people answer with ¿Bueno?; in Spain, ¿Diga? or ¿Sí?.

  • ¿De parte de quién? (Who’s calling?)
  • ¿Me lo repite, por favor? (Could you repeat that, please?)
  • Le marco más tarde. (I’ll call you back later.)

Full guide: {{link:phone-calls-in-spanish|phone calls in Spanish}}.

Ordering food

Restaurant Spanish is all about polite questions. In Spain you will also hear ¿Me pone…? at the bar.

  • ¿Me da unos tacos al pastor, por favor? (Could I have some tacos al pastor, please?)
  • Para llevar, por favor. (To go, please.)
  • La cuenta, por favor. (The check, please.)

Full guide: {{link:ordering-food-in-spanish|ordering food in Spanish}}.

At the doctor

Precision matters here more than anywhere. Learn to describe where it hurts and what you are allergic to.

  • Me duele aquí. (It hurts here.)
  • Tengo fiebre desde ayer. (I’ve had a fever since yesterday.)
  • Soy alérgico a la penicilina. (I’m allergic to penicillin.)

Full guide: {{link:at-the-doctor-in-spanish|at the doctor in Spanish}}.

{{image:3}}

Work and social life

Professional Spanish has its own rules, and it is usually more formal than workplace English in the United States. Expect usted with clients and senior people, and complete sentences in writing. For video calls at work, see {{link:spanish-for-online-meetings|Spanish for online meetings}}.

Writing emails

Spanish emails are more formal than American ones, and their openings and closings follow set patterns.

  • Estimada Sra. López: (Dear Ms. López,)
  • Espero que se encuentre bien. (I hope you’re well.)
  • Quedo a la espera de su respuesta. (I look forward to hearing from you.)

Full guide: {{link:writing-emails-in-spanish|writing emails in Spanish}}.

Talking to coworkers

Office Spanish is friendly and relaxed, usually with tú among colleagues.

  • ¿Tienes un minuto? (Do you have a minute?)
  • ¿Me echas la mano con esto? (Can you give me a hand with this?)
  • ¡Buen trabajo! (Great job!)

Full guide: {{link:talking-to-coworkers-in-spanish|talking to coworkers in Spanish}}.

Job interviews

Interviews call for usted, clear answers about your experience and a good question at the end.

  • Tengo cinco años de experiencia en ventas. (I have five years of experience in sales.)
  • Me considero una persona organizada. (I consider myself an organized person.)
  • ¿Cuáles serían mis responsabilidades? (What would my responsibilities be?)

Full guide: {{link:job-interview-in-spanish|job interview in Spanish}}.

Polite requests

Softening a request is what separates “understood” from “pleasant to deal with”.

  • ¿Podría ayudarme, por favor? (Could you help me, please?)
  • ¿Sería posible cambiar la fecha? (Would it be possible to change the date?)
  • Quisiera hacer una cita. (I’d like to make an appointment.)

Full guide: {{link:polite-requests-in-spanish|polite requests in Spanish}}.

Disagreeing politely

You can disagree in Spanish without sounding rude, as long as you acknowledge the other view first.

  • Entiendo tu punto, pero… (I see your point, but…)
  • No estoy del todo de acuerdo. (I don’t completely agree.)
  • ¿Y si lo intentamos de otra manera? (What if we try it another way?)

Full guide: {{link:disagreeing-politely-in-spanish|disagreeing politely in Spanish}}.

Travel

Travel phrases are everywhere online, so I focus on the moments where precision matters most. The full trip is covered: {{link:at-the-airport-in-spanish|at the airport in Spanish}}, {{link:hotel-spanish-phrases|Spanish hotel phrases}}, {{link:asking-for-directions-in-spanish|asking for directions in Spanish}}, {{link:taking-a-taxi-in-spanish|taking a taxi in Spanish}} and, for longer stays, {{link:renting-an-apartment-in-spanish|renting an apartment in Spanish}}.

Emergencies

In Mexico, as in the US, the emergency number is 911; in Spain and the rest of the European Union it is 112. Learn these before you need them.

  • ¡Ayuda! (Help!)
  • Llame al 911, por favor. (Please call 911.)
  • Necesito una ambulancia. (I need an ambulance.)

Full guide: {{link:emergency-phrases-in-spanish|emergency phrases in Spanish}}.

Messages ready to send

Some moments don’t need a conversation, just the right message. These guides collect dozens of texts you can copy, with translations and notes on tone: {{link:good-morning-messages-in-spanish|good morning messages in Spanish}}, {{link:good-night-messages-in-spanish|good night messages in Spanish}}, {{link:anniversary-messages-in-spanish|anniversary messages in Spanish}}, {{link:valentines-day-messages-in-spanish|Valentine’s Day messages in Spanish}}, {{link:mothers-day-messages-in-spanish|Mother’s Day messages in Spanish}} and {{link:fathers-day-messages-in-spanish|Father’s Day messages in Spanish}}. For the slang you will see in casual chats, see {{link:spanish-slang|Spanish slang}}.

Regional differences you will notice

The phrases in this guide follow Mexican and wider Latin American usage, because that is the Spanish you are most likely to hear in the United States. Here is how a few everyday moments differ in Spain.

SituationMexico and much of Latin AmericaSpain
Answering the phone¿Bueno? (Mexico), ¿Aló? (many countries)¿Diga?, ¿Sí?
Greeting kissOne kiss on the cheekTwo kisses
“Let’s meet”¿Nos vemos?¿Quedamos?
“I miss you”Te extrañoTe echo de menos
“Okay”Va, Órale (Mexico), Dale (many countries)Vale
“You all”ustedesvosotros (informal), ustedes (formal)
Main mealLa comida, often 2–4 p.m. in MexicoLunch, around 2–3 p.m.

These differences add flavor; they rarely cause real misunderstanding. I explore them in depth in {{link:latin-american-vs-spain-spanish|Latin American vs Spain Spanish}}.

Mistakes that cause trouble in any situation

Some mistakes appear again and again, whatever the situation. Knowing them in advance saves a lot of blushing:

  • Estoy embarazada for “I’m embarrassed”. It means pregnant. Say me da vergüenza.
  • Estoy caliente for “I’m hot”. It means aroused. Say tengo calor.
  • Estoy excitado for “I’m excited”. Usually sexual. Say estoy emocionado or tengo muchas ganas.
  • Translating word for word. “I hope this email finds you well” does not work literally; espero que se encuentre bien does.
  • Being too direct. Dame el pan sounds rude at a family table; ¿Me pasas el pan, por favor? sounds natural.

Many of these come from false friends, words that look like English but mean something else. I list thirty of them in {{link:spanish-false-friends|Spanish false friends}}, and the full list of mistakes is in {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|common Spanish mistakes}}.

What translation taught me about everyday Spanish

When I translate a message, the dictionary is the last thing I open. I start with three questions: who is speaking, who is listening and what the message needs to achieve. A thank-you note to a grandmother, a complaint to a landlord and a text to a friend can all be about the same thing and still need completely different Spanish.

The same questions work for learners. Before a conversation, ask yourself how formal it is, what you want to happen and how the other person is likely to feel. Then pick your phrases. That is the logic behind every guide in this series, and it is also why each guide includes a sample conversation, not just a list.

Listening is half of every situation

Phrase guides focus on what to say, but in real life you will spend more time listening. People talk fast, drop sounds and use local expressions. A few lifesavers help in every situation: ¿Me lo repite, por favor? (Could you repeat that, please?), Más despacio, por favor (More slowly, please) and ¿Qué significa…? (What does … mean?). Nobody minds being asked; most people are delighted that you are trying.

How to practice situation by situation

  1. Pick one upcoming moment in your life: a dinner, a call, a birthday.
  2. Read the guide for that situation and choose five phrases you will really use.
  3. Say them aloud and adapt them to your own life and the people involved.
  4. Use them, then note what people said back to you and add it to your notebook.

For checking a word’s meaning or regional use, the Diccionario de la lengua española marks many words by country. And if you want to see everyday Spanish used in full stories, reading side by side in both languages helps; see {{link:parallel-text-reading|parallel text reading}}.

Final thoughts

Spanish becomes yours in real moments: the first mucho gusto to your partner’s mother, the birthday message that makes a friend smile, the kind words that comfort someone you love. This guide will keep growing, one situation at a time. Start with the moment closest to your life this week.

faq.q: What are the most useful Spanish phrases for everyday situations?
faq.a: Greetings (buenos días, mucho gusto), polite requests (¿me da…?, ¿podría…?), apologies (perdón, disculpe, lo siento), thanks, and survival phrases like ¿me lo repite, por favor? and más despacio, por favor.

faq.q: Should I use tú or usted in everyday situations?
faq.a: Use tú with friends, family and people your age in relaxed settings, and usted with strangers, older people and in professional situations. When unsure, start with usted.

faq.q: Is everyday Spanish different in Mexico and Spain?
faq.a: Some words and habits differ, such as answering the phone with ¿Bueno? in Mexico and ¿Diga? in Spain, or te extraño vs te echo de menos. But speakers understand each other easily.

faq.q: How do I say “I’m sorry” in Spanish?
faq.a: Use perdón for small slips, disculpe to be formal or get someone’s attention, and lo siento when you feel real regret or sympathy.

faq.q: How can I practice everyday Spanish if I don’t live near Spanish speakers?
faq.a: Prepare phrases for situations you can recreate: video calls, texting, writing emails or ordering at a local Mexican restaurant. Read and listen to everyday dialogue, and say model conversations aloud.

faq.q: What should I say if I don’t understand someone?
faq.a: Say ¿Me lo repite, por favor? or Más despacio, por favor. Asking politely is normal, and most people are happy to help.
